title: No act without Christ's grace is truly good before God: 'splendid sins'
source_text: XI. Verum communi consensu statuunt Protestantes nullum bonum morale in hoc statu naturae corruptae, sine gratia Christi, ab homine sic perfici posse, ut actio coram Deo revera bona & justa habeatur, neque peccatis debeat accenseri. Ac proinde quaecunque ab hominibus sine Christi gratia fiunt, ut ut speciem virtutis habeant, & externam aliquam bonitatem atque honestatem, peccati rationem in judicio Dei non effugere; adeoque pulcherrima & illustrissima heroum facinora, splendida esse peccata, larvas & simulachra virtutum: ut cum Augustino loquitur saepe jam dictus Morus thesi 42. Bellarminus, inquit, per moralia opera, quae Deo jucunda sunt & qualia Deus postulat, intellexit: quo sensu plane nihil hominem posse, atque adeo pulcherrima ipsius & illustrissima facinora splendida, esse peccata, larvas & simulachra virtutum Augustino facile credimus. Quibus conforme est quod apud Davidem Paraeum legitur, Dicimus, inquit, morales non renatorum virtutes qualescunque, sine fide cum immunditia cordis factas, ut maxime coram mundo sint honestae, justae, laude & praemiis dignae: tamen coram Deo esse peccata, non quidem suo genere, sed per accidens. In lib. 5. Bellar. de gratia & libero Arbitrio, cap. 4. Dicit autem tales virtutes esse peccata per accidens, quoniam licet res sint ex suo genere bonae, in quibusdam tamen essentialibus deficiunt: nempe quia nec ex debito principio oriuntur, nec referuntur in legitimum finem.
pass_a_gloss: XI. But by common consent the Protestants lay down that no moral good in this state of corrupted nature, without the grace of Christ, can by man be so performed, that the action before God be held truly good and just, nor ought to be reckoned among sins. And therefore whatever things by men without Christ's grace are done, however much they have the appearance of virtue, and some external goodness and honesty, do not escape the character of sin in God's judgement; and so the most beautiful and most illustrious deeds of heroes, are splendid sins, masks and images of virtues: as with Augustine speaks the often already mentioned Morus thesis 42. Bellarmine, he says, by moral works, which are pleasing to God and such as God demands, understood: in which sense plainly that man can do nothing, and so that his most beautiful and most illustrious deeds are splendid sins, masks and images of virtues we readily believe Augustine. With which conforms what is read in David Pareus, We say, he says, that the moral virtues of the unregenerate whatever they are, done without faith with uncleanness of heart, however much before the world they be honest, just, worthy of praise and rewards: yet before God are sins, not indeed by their kind, but by accident. On book 5 of Bellarmine on grace and free Choice, chap. 4. But he says such virtues are sins by accident, because although they be things by their kind good, yet in certain essentials they fall short: namely because they neither arise from a due principle, nor are referred to the lawful end.
pass_b_english: Thesis XI. The Protestants, however, hold with one accord that in this state of corrupted nature no moral good can be performed by man without the grace of Christ in such a way that the act is held truly good and just before God and is not to be counted among sins. So whatever men do without the grace of Christ, however much it has the look of virtue and some outward goodness and uprightness, does not escape the character of sin in God's judgement. Thus the finest and most glorious deeds of heroes are splendid sins, masks and likenesses of virtues, as Morus, often cited already, puts it with Augustine in thesis 42.

'By moral works,' he says, 'Bellarmine meant works that please God and such as God requires. In that sense we readily believe Augustine that man can do nothing at all, and that even his finest and most glorious deeds are splendid sins, masks and likenesses of virtues.' What we read in David Pareus agrees with this: 'We say that the moral virtues of the unregenerate, of whatever kind, done without faith and with an unclean heart, however upright, just and worthy of praise and reward they may be before the world, are nonetheless sins before God, not in their kind but by accident' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).

He calls such virtues sins by accident because, though they are good things in their kind, they fall short in certain essentials. They do not arise from the proper principle, and they are not referred to the lawful end.
